reply.text:
The train lurches out of Delhi an hour late. Rain runs sideways across the window. A young woman in a field jacket is standing in the aisle with her bag on her shoulder, looking at the lower berth by the window, and then at you, sitting on it.

"You're in my seat," she says. "Well. You're in the seat I wanted. Different thing."

Across the bay an old man in a white kurta lowers his newspaper to watch.

move.text: I get up, swing my bag onto the upper berth, and point at the window seat. All yours. I only wanted it for the view, and it is dark.

reply.text:
She doesn't thank him right away. She looks at the seat, then at him, then at the dark glass where the rain is coming down in long slanting threads, as if checking that what he said about the view is true. Then she drops her bag onto the berth, sits, and pulls her braid over one shoulder so it won't catch on the window latch.

"That was very fast," she says. "People who give things up that fast usually want something later. Or they're just like that, which is worse, because then you can't even be annoyed with them." She unhooks the binoculars from her neck and lays them in her lap, both hands on them. "Thank you. I'm not giving it back if you change your mind at Panipat."

Across the bay the old man folds his newspaper into a neat square and sets it on his knee. He unscrews the cap of a steel thermos with great care and pours tea into it, steam curling up and fogging the lower half of his reading glasses. "Upper berth is the better berth," he announces, to nobody in particular and to all of them. "Lower berth, everybody sits on you till midnight. Somebody's mother, somebody's tiffin, somebody's goat once, on this very line, nineteen eighty-seven. Upper berth, you are king. Nobody climbs up to disturb a king." He blows on the tea and looks up at Ishaan over the rims. "But the young man has given the window to the girl, so he is a gentleman, and gentlemen sleep badly. That is also a rule."

Meera snorts, very quietly, into her collar. The train shudders over a set of points and the lights blink once, twice, and steady. Somewhere down the carriage a chai seller's voice is already starting up, *chai, chai garam*, though there is no station for miles. The old man raises his thermos cap toward the upper berth like an offering, or a question, and waits.

move.text: I take the tea from him and sit on the edge of the lower berth for a minute. The goat, I say. I need to hear about the goat.

reply.text:
Uncle Bhalla's whole face rearranges itself. He sets the thermos down between his feet, takes off his reading glasses, wipes the fog from them with the hem of his kurta, and puts them back on, all of it slow and deliberate, a man who has been waiting a long time for exactly this question. "The goat," he says. "Nineteen eighty-seven. No. Eighty-six. Monsoon, like this, I was posted at Ambala Cantt, booking window number three, which was the bad window, because number three is next to the toilet." He holds up a finger. "That is not part of the story. That is only so you understand my condition at the time. So. A family gets on at Sonipat, husband, wife, wife's mother, four children, and one goat. White goat, brown face. And the TT comes, Sharma, very strict man, his father was also TT, on the Frontier Mail, before Partition, that man once put a minister off at Lahore for no ticket." He pauses, frowning at the window. "Or Amritsar. Anyway. Sharma says, where is the ticket for the animal. And the grandmother says," and here he leans forward and drops his voice into a reedy falsetto, "*which animal?*"

Meera has drawn her knees up onto the berth to make room, and she is watching Bhalla with her chin on her binoculars, the way she might watch a bird do something she hadn't read about. The train sways. Rain finds a gap in the window frame and beads along the sill beside her elbow; she doesn't move it away. Bhalla is now explaining that the goat had been put into a bedding roll, and that Sharma could see the bedding roll breathing, but that the grandmother had sat on it, and then he stops to explain that a bedding roll is not like these modern things, it was canvas, proper canvas, his own was from his father-in-law and lasted nineteen years.

"Uncle," Meera says, not unkindly, "did it eat the ticket."

Bhalla looks wounded. "You are skipping." He picks up his thermos again, offended and pleased in equal measure, and pours himself a fresh cap. Meera turns her head and looks at Ishaan instead, plainly, the way she looked at the seat before she took it. Her eyes go to the collar showing at the neck of the hoodie, crisp, still holding the line of an iron, and back up to his face. "Where are you actually going?" she says. "Not the station. I mean what's at the end of it. You've got the face of someone going to a wedding he's not invited to. Or one he is invited to, which is worse." Across the bay, Bhalla stops blowing on his tea, and waits too.

move.text: I glance at Meera. And you, what are the binoculars for? Bird watching in the dark seems ambitious.

reply.text:
Meera doesn't answer straight away. She looks at him a beat longer than the question needs, one eyebrow going up a fraction and settling again, the look of someone writing a note in a margin to come back to later. Then she lifts the binoculars an inch off her knees, as if they could speak for themselves.

"I count birds," she says. "That's the job. Somebody has to, or nobody knows they're gone until they're gone." She turns the focus wheel with her thumb, idly, though there is nothing to focus on. "Kalka, and then up into the hills. A month. Transects at five in the morning, which means I'll be asleep by nine every night and talking to no one, which is fine." The last word comes out a little flat. "And it's not ambitious. Plenty of things are awake in the dark. Nightjars. Some of the thrushes, before light. You just listen more than you look."

"Owls," says Bhalla, with authority, setting his cap of tea on the little folding table as if calling a meeting to order. "At Barog station there was an owl that sat on the signal post every night for six years. Every night. The stationmaster named it. Pandit-ji, because it looked at everyone like they had made a mistake in their accounts." He nods at Meera. "You will see him. Not him, he is dead now, obviously, but his family. Owls keep the same posts. More loyal than staff." He seems ready to go on, about Barog, about the tunnel, about the British engineer who shot himself there, but the train leans into a long curve and he has to put a hand out for his thermos.

Meera has already turned to the window. She cups one hand against the glass to cut the reflection of the carriage lights and looks out past it, into fields that aren't there, only black and the rain drawn across it in silver threads, a single lamp somewhere far off sliding away. Her breath fogs a small circle on the pane and fades. Without turning round she says, to the glass more than to anyone, "You still haven't said where you're going." The rain ticks along the sill between her elbow and Ishaan's knee, and the chai seller's voice comes closer down the aisle.

move.text: I tell her I am going to Shimla for a job interview I do not want, and that I have not told anyone that part.

reply.text:
Meera takes her hand away from the glass. The little circle of fog she left there shrinks and goes. She doesn't turn round at once, and when she does she doesn't smile, and she doesn't say *why* or *then why go*. She looks at him the way she looked at the empty fields, as though there might be something out there if she waited long enough. Then she reaches down, unzips one of the many pockets on her jacket, a low one near the hem, and takes out a small packet of Parle-G gone soft at the corners. She tears it open along the top and holds it out across the gap between them, the rain still ticking on the sill beside her elbow.

"For the tea," she says. That's all.

Bhalla has heard every word, because Bhalla hears everything on this line. He sets his cap down on the folding table with a small click. "Interview," he says, as if naming a disease he has had and recovered from. "Nineteen seventy-four I sat for the railway interview. Did not want it. My father wanted it. My father sat outside the hall for four hours in the sun with a tiffin so I would not run away." He takes off his glasses and lets them drop on their string against his chest. "Thirty-four years I sat at that window. Wanting is for films. You go, you sit, you answer, they decide. Afterwards you decide." He considers this, then adds, more quietly, to his thermos rather than to anyone, "Some people decide too late. That is also allowed."

The chai seller comes down the aisle with a dented aluminium kettle in one hand and a tower of paper cups in the other, swaying with the carriage like he's been born to its rhythm, a thin boy of maybe seventeen in a rain-dark shirt. "Chai, chai garam. Didi? Uncle?" Meera holds up two fingers, then glances at Ishaan's cap, already half drunk, and makes it three. She is digging in another pocket for change when Bhalla waves a hand over the whole bay like a man signing off a ledger and pushes a twenty and a ten into the boy's palm. "Mine," he says. "On my line, I pay." The boy pours three cups in one long practised stream, the steam rising grey under the carriage lights, and hands one to each of them. He is already moving off down the aisle, *chai, chai*, before anyone can argue.

Meera wraps both hands round her cup and doesn't drink yet. The biscuit packet is still open on her knee between them. Outside, a level crossing goes by, a single yellow lamp and a man under an umbrella on a cycle, waiting, and then the dark again. "Thirty-four years," she says to Bhalla, and then, without quite looking at Ishaan, "What time is it? The interview."

move.text: Eleven tomorrow, I say, and take a biscuit. Then I ask her what she is going to count up there for a month.

reply.text:
"Everything that'll stand still long enough," Meera says, and then, because that isn't true, she sets her cup on the sill and starts counting on her fingers. "Laughingthrushes, three kinds if I'm lucky. Minivets, the scarlet ones, they go through the canopy in little gangs like schoolboys. Himalayan bulbuls, which are everywhere and nobody cares about, so I care about them. And cheer pheasant, which is the real reason they're paying me. Maybe a few hundred left on those slopes. Maybe fewer. You hear them before light, this awful crowing, like a rusty gate somebody keeps opening." She's leaning forward now without noticing it, the braid sliding off her shoulder. "You walk a fixed line, same line, same time, every morning, and you write down every call. Thirty days of the same walk. That's how you know if something's changed." She picks up a biscuit herself and turns it over. "My mother has red-whiskered bulbuls on her balcony in Pune. Two of them. She's named them, which I told her you're not supposed to do." She stops, dunks the biscuit too long, and it breaks off into the tea. She looks at the soggy half in the cup with exaggerated disgust and fishes for it with two fingers. "Anyway. Pheasants."

"Pheasants," Bhalla says, with deep scepticism, as if she had said *tigers*. "In Kalka you will not see a pheasant. In Kalka you will see monkeys. Monkeys will take your binoculars, your tiffin, your spectacles, your dignity." He taps his own glasses on their string for emphasis. "Nineteen ninety-one a monkey took the stationmaster's register off the platform at Kalka and sat on the roof of the toy train reading it. Nobody could get it down till Dharampur." He means to go on. His mouth opens for it. Instead a yawn takes him, enormous and unashamed, the whole jaw cracking, and he covers it late with the back of his hand and looks faintly betrayed by his own body. "Eleven o'clock," he announces. "On this line, eleven o'clock is the rule."

As if it heard him, the carriage begins to dim from the far end. Someone pulls a switch two bays down and the tube light there goes out; then another, closer. Curtains of blue night-glow replace the white. People shift and murmur, a child complains and is shushed, a man somewhere is already snoring in long, wet, confident pulls. Bhalla stands, one knee popping, and starts unrolling a sheet onto his lower berth with the fussy precision of a man who has made a thousand railway beds, tucking the corners under the green rexine. "Upper berth," he says, nodding up at Ishaan's bag without looking, "you will want to go up before I put the light off. Climbing in the dark, that is how gentlemen break their necks."

Meera hasn't moved from the window. She has her cup in both hands again, the biscuit half drowned at the bottom of it, and the blue light makes her look younger and more tired. The rain has thinned to a fine slant. She looks at Ishaan, at the folded collar, at the biscuit in his hand, and she doesn't say goodnight. "Eleven," she says instead, quietly, under the snoring. "So you'll get to Kalka, take the toy train, sleep in some guest house, iron that shirt again, and go and sit in a room and say yes to things." It isn't quite a question. She waits, as if this is the part of the transect where you stop walking and just listen.

move.text: Later, when Bhalla starts snoring, I climb up to my berth and say goodnight to her through the gap in the curtain.

reply.text:
Bhalla snores the way he tells stories, with long preambles and sudden emphatic stops, as if waiting for someone to ask what happened next. Each one ends in a small whistle through the nose and a smack of the lips, then a pause long enough to make the bay wonder, then he starts again. His glasses have slid off his chest on their string and swing a little with the train, ticking against the edge of the berth. The thermos stands upright on the floor between his chappals, capped, guarded even in his sleep.

For a while nothing comes back through the curtain. The blue night-light hums. Two bays down the confident snorer has found a partner, and the two of them trade off in the dark like a duet that has rehearsed. Below, there is the dry sound of a page, or a sheet, or a packet of biscuits being folded shut and tucked back into a pocket, and a zip running closed.

"Goodnight," Meera says at last. It comes up low and late, flat at the edges, the way she said *fine* earlier about talking to no one. Then, after the train has crossed something hollow, a culvert or a small bridge, and the sound has gone out from under them and come back: "I'm not sleepy. I'm never sleepy the first night. I lie there and count stations." A short breath that might be a laugh at herself. "Don't tell Uncle. He'll make it a rule."

The berth creaks as she turns onto her side, toward the window. Through the gap in the curtain there is only the top of her braid against the pillow she has made of her jacket, and the faint pale smear where her forehead nearly touches the glass. Outside, the rain has thinned to almost nothing, a fine grey slant that catches the light of each passing pole and lets it go. The wheels go on under all of them, steady, unhurried, counting the joints of the track toward Ambala, and somewhere ahead a horn sounds once, long, into the dark, and Meera does not move from the window.
